features.name: North Equatorial Belt
features.description: One of Jupiter's most prominent dark bands, the North Equatorial Belt is a wide region of sinking, compressed air that appears reddish-brown due to complex organic compounds and phosphine chemistry. It is one of the most consistently visible features in any amateur telescope.

details.label: Width
details.value: Spans roughly 15° to 25° north latitude

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The NEB occasionally 'fades', turning white for months at a time before returning — scientists still do not fully understand why.

features.name: South Equatorial Belt
features.description: The southern counterpart to the NEB and arguably even more dynamic, the South Equatorial Belt is home to powerful jet streams and is where the Great Red Spot is embedded. It has dramatically faded and revived multiple times in recorded history.

details.label: Width
details.value: Spans roughly 7° to 27° south latitude

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: In 2010 the SEB faded almost completely white before erupting back to full colour — a dramatic transformation visible through backyard telescopes.

features.name: North Temperate Belt
features.description: A mid-latitude dark belt in Jupiter's northern hemisphere, the North Temperate Belt marks a boundary between opposing jet streams. It often shows festoons, barges, and white ovals along its edges.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Dark 'barges' — long, reddish-brown oval features — drift slowly along the NTB and can persist for years.

features.name: Equatorial Zone
features.description: The bright equatorial zone is a region of rising air that cools to form white ammonia-ice clouds. It sits between the North and South Equatorial Belts and is crossed by dramatic dark festoons that dip down from the NEB.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The dark festoons draping into the EZ are caused by wave-driven downwelling and are among the most complex weather patterns in the Solar System.

features.name: Great Red Spot
features.description: The Great Red Spot is an anticyclonic storm that has raged for at least 350 years, making it the longest-lived storm known in the Solar System. Wind speeds at its edges exceed 400 km/h. It has been shrinking steadily over the last century and is now roughly 1.3 times the diameter of Earth.

details.label: Storm age
details.value: Observed continuously since the 1870s; possibly older

details.label: Current size
details.value: Approximately 16,000 km across as of the 2020s

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: In the 1800s the GRS was so large that three Earths could have fit inside it side by side.

features.name: Oval BA
features.description: Oval BA — nicknamed 'Red Spot Jr.' — formed between 1998 and 2000 when three white ovals merged into one. It later turned red, suggesting it had deepened enough to dredge up the same chromophores that give the Great Red Spot its colour.

details.label: Formation
details.value: Merged from three white ovals: FA, BC, and DE

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The merging of three long-lived storms into one was the first time such an event was observed in real time on any planet.

features.name: North Polar Cyclone Cluster
features.description: NASA's Juno spacecraft revealed that Jupiter's north pole hosts a central cyclone surrounded by eight circumpolar cyclones arranged in a near-perfect geometric pattern. These massive storms are each roughly the size of the continental United States.

details.label: Discovery
details.value: First imaged by Juno in 2017

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Despite their close proximity, the polar cyclones have remained stably spaced for years — a behaviour that puzzles atmospheric scientists.

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: Jupiter's north polar region is a chaotic, blue-tinted area unlike anything seen at lower latitudes. The familiar banded structure dissolves here into a complex of turbulent filaments and oval storms. Juno's infrared observations show deep heat radiating from below.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Jupiter's northern aurora is powered by Io's volcanic activity, which pumps charged sulphur and oxygen ions into the magnetic field.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: The south pole hosts five circumpolar cyclones arranged around a central storm — a slightly different geometry from the eight in the north. Bright auroral ovals ring the pole, powered by the electromagnetic coupling between Jupiter and its moons, especially Io.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The south polar cyclone cluster rotates as a stable unit, with the storms 'bouncing' elastically off one another rather than merging.

features.name: Main Ring
features.description: Jupiter's Main Ring is a thin, flat disc of fine dust particles shed by the inner moons Metis and Adrastea when meteorites strike their surfaces. Discovered by Voyager 1 in 1979, it extends from about 122,500 km to 129,000 km from Jupiter's centre and is only about 30 km thick.

details.label: Discovered
details.value: Voyager 1, 1979

details.label: Thickness
details.value: Approximately 30 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Jupiter's rings are so faint they were completely unknown before Voyager — Earth-based telescopes had no hope of detecting them.

features.name: Halo Ring
features.description: The innermost of Jupiter's rings, the Halo Ring is a thick, faint torus of dust that extends inward from the Main Ring to about 100,000 km from Jupiter's centre. It puffs out vertically due to electromagnetic forces pushing charged dust particles out of the equatorial plane.

details.label: Thickness
details.value: Up to 20,000 km vertically

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Halo Ring glows slightly brighter when viewed from certain angles — a phenomenon called forward scattering that reveals its fine dust composition.

features.name: Gossamer Rings
features.description: The Gossamer Rings are two faint, broad rings outside the Main Ring, sourced from dust knocked off the moons Amalthea and Thebe. They are extremely tenuous — hundreds of times fainter than the Main Ring — and were only fully resolved by the Galileo spacecraft in the 1990s.

details.label: Source moons
details.value: Amalthea and Thebe

details.label: Discovered fully
details.value: Galileo spacecraft, 1990s

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The two Gossamer Rings have sharp outer edges that align almost exactly with the orbits of Amalthea and Thebe, confirming those moons as the dust source.

features.name: Adrastea
features.description: Adrastea is one of Jupiter's tiny inner moons and orbits right at the outer boundary of the Main Ring. Its surface is a likely source of the fine dust that keeps the Main Ring supplied after impacts loft particles away from the moon.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Main Ring boundary

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 16 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Adrastea orbits Jupiter faster than the planet rotates, completing a circuit in roughly seven hours.

features.name: Amalthea
features.description: Amalthea is the largest of Jupiter's inner moons, a reddish, irregular body orbiting inside the gossamer ring region. Dust knocked from Amalthea helps feed the inner gossamer ring, placing the moon visually between the Main Ring and the broader outer dust sheet.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Inner Gossamer Ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 167 km along its longest axis

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Amalthea is strongly red, likely from material altered by Jupiter's radiation environment and sulphur from Io.

features.name: Thebe
features.description: Thebe is a small, irregular moon embedded in the outer gossamer ring region. Its orbit lines up with the faint outer dust band, making it one of the source worlds that gives Jupiter's ring system its broad, delicate outer edge.

details.label: Ring position
details.value: Outer Gossamer Ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 98 km along its longest axis

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Thebe has a huge impact basin named Zethus, a scar that takes up a large fraction of the moon's surface.
